title: Kushner Shuttles Between Hamas and Netanyahu, But Gaza Ceasefire Road Map Stalls
summary:
The diplomatic shuttle is in high gear, but the gears are grinding. Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and Mideast negotiator, held an hourslong meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem on Monday, just one day after sitting down with Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya in Cairo. The back-to-back talks are part of an intense U.S. push to salvage a 15-point road map designed to move the Gaza ceasefire forward—but the two sides remain far apart.

Hamas says it has agreed to the road map, which includes disarmament and a "credible pathway toward achieving Palestinian self-determination and statehood." The group is urging mediators and the U.S.-created Board of Peace to "compel" Israel to sign on. Israel, however, insists that Hamas must fully disarm before any Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. Under the road map, Israel would gradually pull back its forces, but Netanyahu's government rejects the statehood component outright.

The stakes are enormous. Some 2 million Palestinians remain in Gaza, many living in tent camps amid widespread destruction. Israeli forces currently control about 60 percent of the enclave, and Netanyahu has spoken of expanding that to 70 percent, "tightening the grip" on Hamas. Reconstruction and the deployment of international forces are on hold until the road map is agreed to.

Regional frustration is mounting. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia, and the ceasefire mediators issued a joint statement condemning Israel's rejection, saying Israel "now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza." They called on the Board of Peace and the U.S. to take "immediate and concrete measures" to keep any party from blocking implementation.

Netanyahu faces a challenging election on October 27, with coalition partners who take a hard line on Gaza. That political pressure may make decisive action on the ceasefire unlikely before then. Meanwhile, ordinary Gazans are skeptical. "A conference here and there, it is all lies," said Mohammad Abu al-Qombuz, who lives in a Gaza City tent camp. "We need a definitive solution that would work for everybody." As the anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attack approaches, the path to peace remains as tangled as ever.
why_it_matters: The ceasefire road map is not just about diplomacy; it tests whether a negotiated sequence of disarmament and withdrawal can end a war, shape Palestinian self-rule, and prevent another regional escalation—issues that will define the Middle East for young people's generation.

background_read: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and former White House adviser, has returned as a Mideast negotiator, shuttling between Cairo and Jerusalem.
Hamas, a Palestinian militant group that has governed Gaza since 2007 and is designated a terrorist organisation by the United States and European Union, has survived repeated conflicts with Israel.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, leads a right-wing coalition that includes hardline partners opposed to Palestinian statehood.
The Gaza war began after Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel; since then much of Gaza has been destroyed and most of its roughly 2 million residents have been displaced.
The Board of Peace, a U.S.-created body mentioned in the road map, is meant to oversee implementation of the ceasefire plan.

perspectives.perspective: Israeli government and hardline coalition partners
perspectives.description: They see full disarmament before withdrawal as a necessary security condition, because allowing Hamas to keep weapons could invite future attacks. They also reject any road map that grants Palestinian statehood, viewing it as rewarding violence and threatening Israel's security.

perspectives.perspective: Hamas, Gazan civilians, and supportive regional states
perspectives.description: They argue Israel is obstructing a peace plan that Hamas has accepted, prolonging displacement and blocking reconstruction. Ordinary Gazans like Mohammad Abu al-Qombuz see the conferences as empty promises and demand a definitive solution.

They focus on sequencing: the road map requires simultaneous trust between parties that do not trust each other. Mediators can arrange shuttle diplomacy and issue statements, but without enforcement power the Board of Peace may not compel either side to implement the plan.

They warn that Netanyahu's October 27 election and the October 7 anniversary make near-term concessions less likely. If the road map collapses, they foresee more fighting, a larger Israeli security zone, and deeper regional frustration.
